description: We are a multidisciplinary team passionate about space, technology, AI, and data. Our team combines skills in data analysis, app development, UI/UX design, graphic design, and creative problem-solving. We aim to collaborate, innovate, and build a meaningful solution that turns NASA data into real-world impact.
summary:
CityPulse aims to provide a practical approach to understanding environmental and urban changes by transforming satellite data into clear accessible and comparable information

Our team developed an interactive application that allows users to track changes in land surface temperature vegetation cover and urban expansion over different time periods Through interactive maps and visual indicators the application makes it easier to identify and analyze environmental patterns

The project addresses the Be an Earth System Trend Detective challenge by using Earth observation data to detect environmental trends understand how they evolve and examine their impacts

The key outcomes of the project include enabling comparisons of environmental changes over time highlighting areas experiencing rising temperatures or declining vegetation and identifying urban expansion patterns and their relationship with the surrounding environment These findings are presented through clear visualizations that simplify data interpretation and help identify areas requiring greater attention

CityPulse bridges the gap between scientific data and practical applications by supporting environmental research urban planning and data driven decision making

Ultimately our goal is to contribute to building more sustainable and resilient cities that are better prepared to face future environmental changes and challenges
details:
What does it do?

CityPulse is a mobile web app that lets anyone see how Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam have changed over the years, through NASA satellite data. You search for your district, see it on a live satellite map, and compare it between two years, anywhere from 2013 to 2025. You can switch between land surface temperature, vegetation (NDVI) and a true-colour view, so it’s easy to spot where it got hotter or where green areas disappeared. The Insights page turns those readings into a short summary you can download as a PDF. We also added Pulse AI, an assistant you can just ask things like “how has my area changed?” in Arabic or English, and it can even read the answer out loud.

Why does it matter?

Our cities are growing fast, and that growth is changing how hot our neighbourhoods feel and how much green space we have left. Satellite data can show this clearly, but it’s usually hard for regular people to read. We wanted to change that. Our goal is to help residents understand their own neighbourhoods, and to give planners a simple way to see which districts need more trees or shade.

How we built it

We built the app with JavaScript and React, along with HTML, CSS and some Python to prepare the data. We used Leaflet for the maps, Vite and Node.js to build and run the app, and Vercel to host it. Pulse AI runs on the Google Gemini API. The imagery and readings come from NASA: Landsat, Sentinel-2 (HLS) and MODIS, through NASA GIBS, ORNL DAAC and Microsoft Planetary Computer. District locations come from OpenStreetMap. We didn’t need any special hardware, just our laptops, and we tested on our phones.

What makes it creative?

What we like most is how it brings several NASA datasets together in one place that feels easy and friendly. Instead of charts and raw numbers, you see your own street change over more than ten years. And if something isn’t clear, you can simply ask Pulse AI in your own language.

What we thought about along the way

Accuracy: every reading comes from NASA, never made up. We picked cloud-free images and left water out of the averages so the numbers stay fair.

Ease of use: the app works on any phone browser without installing anything, in Arabic and English, and covers every district in the three cities.

Safety and speed: we kept the AI key on the server, and kept the app light so it loads fast on phones.
